sentences.gloss_en: Welcome to our new explainer.
Today's goal isn't just memorizing some code or syntax tricks.
We're here to build a real mental model of how Python works from the inside.
We'll see how code breathes, step by step.
We'll rely mainly on the code-trace technique.
The current line is lit, next to it a names panel with arrows pointing to values, and stack frames rising and falling in front of us.
Ready? Let's start the journey.
Our agenda is quick and dense.
We start with memory and control basics, then loops and functions, data structures and their cost, key interview cards, and finally saving data and virtual environments.
Let's jump straight into the first section.
Memory basics, and how control flow really works.
In other programming languages we might picture a variable as a box we put a value into.
But in Python it's completely different.
A variable here isn't a magic box.
In the code trace in front of us, see the highlighted line?
The name price is bound by an arrow to the value 100, and the name qty by an arrow to the value 3.
When we compute total, a new arrow is created pointing to the value 300.
That arrow means identity.
Since every value has a type, like numbers or text, it's very important to validate user input.
Because if someone types a word instead of the number, things break on us if we haven't planned for it.
Now, as for control flow...
Picture it as a pointer walking along a road with forks, based on the conditions we set.
For example, classifying customers: VIPs paid 10,000 or more, Gold 5,000, and Silver 1,000.
The pointer takes the first branch whose condition is true.
That's why the order here is decisive.
If we put the 1,000 condition first, the pointer enters it immediately and all VIP customers get wrongly classified as Silver.
The other branches stay there, but the pointer never reaches them.
Section two takes us a step deeper: loops, accumulators, and how functions breathe in memory.
Now it's time for our first prediction question; focus with me.
We have a loop running over five orders, and an accumulator named total that sums only the delivered orders, which are three.
Right before the loop's last iteration, what will total be?
Think about it for a few seconds before we flip the slide.
If the answer that came to your mind is 2 or 3, that means your code is sound and excellent.
But if the answer is zero, that reveals a very famous bug we fall into.
If we write total equals zero inside the loop itself, then with every new iteration the variable is wiped and starts from zero again.
So the value before the last iteration will be zero, and the final result will be just the last order's state.
The accumulator must always live outside the loop, and we add inside it.
From loops we move on to functions.
A function is simply a computation we've given a specific name.
As soon as we call it, a dramatic scene happens under the hood: a stack frame rises on top of the stack.
Parameters get bound to arguments.
For instance, if we compute a price with a 15% discount, the value gets bound to 85.
All the work happens inside this frame.
And once the code hits return, the value comes back and the frame vanishes completely, as if it never existed.
Quick note: if we don't write an explicit return, the function returns None automatically.
When we write a variable name, how does Python look it up?
It follows a rule called LEGB, which these nested circles explain simply.
It starts by searching locally, inside the function.
If it doesn't find it, it widens the circle to the enclosing scope, then the global scope across the whole file, and finally the names built into the language itself.
This system prevents any naming confusion.
Now into section three: data structures, and how to pick the right container without paying a high performance cost.
These four containers in front of us are the foundation.
A list is an ordered row: we can modify it, repeat data, and reach any element by index.
A tuple is just like it but locked and unchangeable, which makes it great as a key in a dictionary.
A set is a bag that doesn't care about order at all, but its great feature is that it completely prevents duplicates.
And finally the dictionary maps a key to a value, and since Python 3.7 it preserves insertion order.
And here we reach the second prediction question.
If we want to do an existence check, a membership test, to see whether an element is in a dataset of ten thousand elements or not...
Which one do you think finishes the check faster, the list or the set?
The answer is very clear in the split screen in front of us.
On the left, the list checks in O(n): the pointer walks the elements one by one and the comparison counter keeps counting up to ten thousand.
If this operation sits inside another loop, it could take five minutes.
But look at the right: the set works in O(1); the value is turned into a hash and the pointer goes to its spot in a single step.
The counter stopped at one and the whole operation finished in two seconds.
See how choosing the right data structure saves enormous time?
Today's fourth section gathers the most important technical interview cards, indispensable ones that test our real understanding of the language.
These cards are dense and very important.
For strings we have essential functions like lower and split.
And f-strings like f"${p:.2f}", which format numbers beautifully.
List comprehensions are magic: they let us write a whole loop in a single line.
Like applying a 10% discount by multiplying prices by 0.9: p times 0.9 for p in prices.
Or filtering prices to those above 500: if p is greater than 500.
terms: p for p in prices if p > 500

sentences.gloss_en: And slicing, like colon colon minus 1, which reverses the list instantly.
It's very important to distinguish sorted, which returns a new list, from .sort, which modifies the original list in place.
Let's continue with the rest of the cards.
Sets are excellent for set math: union, intersection and difference.
For example, subtracting the active users from the premium subscribers gives us the users we need to re-engage.
For tuples, to make a tuple with just one element we must add a comma, like one comma.
With dictionaries, always get used to .get, so if the key is missing the code returns a default value instead of throwing a KeyError at us.
And Counter makes it easy to pull the most repeated elements with most_common(3).
The last cards in this section are for advanced collections.
If we want a queue, don't use a plain list; it's always better to use deque.
Because popping and adding at both ends takes a single step (1) with popleft, which is much faster.
And if we always need to pull the smallest value first, heapq, the priority queue, is what saves us.
But if we just want a stack, adding and removing from the end only, a plain list does the job and more.
Section five moves us to saving data, because any data in memory vanishes as soon as the program closes.
To save data we have two ways that are the most popular.
CSV is simply flat rows and columns, simple and found everywhere, like Excel sheets.
The second is JSON, which stands out by allowing nested data.
For example, a purchase order can contain details of many products inside it.
That's why it's the main language of APIs.
But more important than choosing the format is that we always use the with open statement when reading or writing any file.
Why? Because it guarantees the file gets closed properly and we avoid leaking memory even if an error happens midway.
Our sixth and final section: virtual environments, and how to isolate our projects from each other.
A virtual environment is the most important step to isolate this project's libraries from any other project on the machine.
And it puts an end to the line 'the code was working on my machine'.
The steps are very simple: we create the environment with python -m venv .venv and activate it with activate.
We install the libraries we need, like pandas, and most importantly we record all the exact versions using pip freeze and direct it to a requirements.txt file.
Without this file, if we move the code to another machine, a ModuleNotFoundError can show up and everything grinds to a halt.
Applying everything we explained, these are real outputs of a small project we built called ShopFlow.cli.
We split the work into very clear files: a script that computes revenue, revenue.py; an order validator, validate.py; and a customer index using a dictionary, index.py.
And we also have the function called order_total, now organized and fully ready for us to write tests for it in the next stage.
In the end, the most important lesson of this whole journey: master the execution path and understand what happens under the hood before being dazzled by syntax tricks and writing code fast.
Building a strong mental model is what will make you write faster, cleaner, bug-free code.
So which concept do you feel changed your view of how Python works the most, and that you'll apply right away in your next project?
Thank you so much for your time, and see you in the next explainer.
